data.title: Get found by the people already looking for what you make
paragraphs: Someone a few towns over is searching for exactly what you sell. They are typing the fruit, or the cut, or the town. They are not typing specialty food, and that search is finding somebody else.
We write the pages that put you in that result, and we keep writing them, so the catalog you already built starts earning instead of sitting there.

data.title: The search you are already losing

paragraphs: Nobody types specialty food into a search box. They type chokecherry jelly, or dried huckleberries, or guanciale, and most of the time they put a town after it. That is the entire shape of demand in this category, and it is why a beautifully written About page does nothing for you.

Those searches are small, specific, and sit very close to a purchase. There is little competition for them, because most of the industry is still writing about being family owned for three generations. The maker who describes the one thing precisely is the maker who takes the click.
Your catalog is the biggest asset you own for this. Every product you sell is a search somebody runs. Does the page they land on tell them anything they could not have guessed from the photo?

data.title: Where the catalog quits on you
data.subtitle: None of these look like problems from the inside. They look like an ordinary product page.

items.title: Nothing on the page says who made it
items.text: The description covers size, weight, and ingredients, and stops before it reaches the person, the place, or the reason this exists at all.
items.text2: Provenance is the one thing a competitor cannot copy off your site, and it is the part shoppers repeat to somebody else when they hand over the jar.

items.title: Every jar sounds like every other jar
items.text: Small batch, handcrafted, artisanal. Those three words are on every competing page too, so they carry no information and a shopper learns nothing from reading them.
items.text2: Specifics are the only separator left. The fruit, the elevation it grew at, the person who stirs it, the reason it tastes the way it does.

items.title: Most of the catalog was never written
items.text: Six hero products get a written description and the rest keep the supplier's paragraph, which is the identical paragraph on every other site carrying that item.
items.text2: Those are the pages holding the buying intent, because somebody searching one exact product is far closer to paying than somebody browsing a category.

items.title: The gift season starts before you do
items.text: Gift guides go up in November, weeks after the searches that decide the quarter have already been running and already been answered by somebody else.
items.text2: Seasonal pages only pay if they are indexed and ranking before the season opens, which makes the calendar the hardest part of the work.

data.title: What the work looks like in practice

paragraphs: One post a week, on the same day every week. That is most of it. The blog we write for a specialty food maker is past a hundred posts now, and not one of them went up because somebody had a burst of energy in March and then got busy.

A recipe guide on that blog carries three recipes marked up so a search engine reads them as recipes instead of as paragraphs about food. Inside the same post are four product cards pointing at jars a reader can put in a cart, and every one of those links gets checked against stock before the post ships, because a link to a sold-out jar is worse than no link.
That is the job most weeks. Small, specific, checked. It is not glamorous and it is the reason the catalog keeps earning between seasons.

data.title: Found in AI search because a person described it
data.subtitle: Answer engines quote passages they can lift without the passage falling apart, and vague copy does not clear that bar.
